datactr: Says high energy users must pay their fair share and pressed PJM on it, but opposed an early end to data centers' tax break and cut a cost-shift provision (Jan-Apr 2026).
utility: Proposed capping Dominion's profit at 9.3% with excess credited to customers (rejected) and signed utility billing/disconnect protections (Apr 2026).
pricecap: Joined bipartisan PJM governors' push to protect ratepayers; the group has sought extension of the capacity price collar (Apr 2026).
eohousing: Day One executive order launched a multi-agency review of housing rules and permitting to speed approvals (Jan 2026).
trust: Proposed a revolving loan fund for mixed-income housing development, a related financing tool (Jan 2026).
downpay: Signed HB164/SB328 removing caps on employer-assisted homeownership grants; narrower than general down payment aid (Apr 2026).
renter: Proposed extending the eviction response window to two weeks and signed HB15/SB48 tenant protections (Jan-Apr 2026).
childcare: Called for expanding access to Virginia's child care subsidy program, short of universal care (Jan 2026).
teacher: Told the General Assembly Virginia must pay teachers more, 'Period.' (Jan 2026).
ice: Signed SB491 limiting sharing of student immigration data with DHS absent a judicial warrant; amended mask limits on agents (Apr 2026).
guard: Signed SB 337 (Apr 2026), which orders a study of how Virginia should respond to Guard deployments the governor hasn't approved and bars using the Guard to intimidate voters.
npv: Signed HB965 joining the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (Apr 2026).
wage: Signed HB1/SB1 raising Virginia's minimum wage to $13.75 in 2027 and $15 in 2028 (Apr 2026).
house: Signed SB531 requiring localities statewide to allow accessory dwelling units and capping ADU permit costs (Apr 2026).
roe: Told lawmakers she supports the constitutional amendment protecting reproductive freedom; also signed a right-to-contraception law (Jan-Apr 2026).
pfml: Proposed a statewide paid family and medical leave program; her amendments to SB2/HB1207 were accepted and it became law (Apr 2026).

datactr: Signed SB 6231 removing a sales tax exemption for replacing data center equipment; narrower than full cost recovery (Apr 2026).

trust: $244 million for affordable housing, the largest supplemental housing investment (2026).

ctc: Would expand the Working Families Tax Credit with Millionaires' Tax revenue (2026).
millionaire: Proposed a Millionaires' Tax on income over $1 million (Jan 2026).
prek: Touted Ballmer partnership bringing up to $1 billion for free early learning programs; not a universal pre-K pledge (Jan 2026).
childcare: Ballmer Group partnership of up to $1 billion for free early learning (2026).
ice: Signed SB 5855 barring law enforcement, including ICE, from wearing masks on duty; related to, not a sensitive-locations ban (Mar 2026).
guard: Signed HB 1321 (Apr 2025) barring other states' Guard from entering without his permission.
fraud: Executive order created a chief fraud prevention officer and statewide fraud workgroup; plans a state False Claims Act (Oct 2026).

medicaid: Would fully fund the Medicaid rebase, $319 million plus $728 million (2026).
datactr: Spokesperson said Stein has long held that data centers must pay their own way so families don't foot the bill (May 2026).
mctax: Budget would raise the standard deduction to $26,500 while pausing scheduled income tax rate cuts (Apr 2026).
ctc: Proposed a refundable Working Families Tax Credit and a child and dependent care credit (2026).
prek: Budget includes new investment in NC Pre-K, but no universal pre-K pledge (Apr 2026).
childcare: Would raise child care subsidy rates and set a statewide floor (2026).
teacher: Average 11% teacher raise, highest starting pay in the Southeast (Apr 2026 budget).
vouchers: Would phase out the universal Opportunity Scholarship voucher expansion (Apr 2026 budget).
ice: Vetoed HB 318 and SB 153, which expanded state cooperation with ICE (Jun 2025); not a sensitive-locations rule, and he backs ICE alerts for serious crimes.
guard: Signed the Aug 2025 Democratic governors' statement against deployments without consent; sent one Guard member to D.C. for America 250 (2026).

ss.name: Texas
ss.rule: Final passage takes a majority of senators present; the lieutenant governor breaks ties. Under the Senate's current rules a bill can't reach the floor without 5/9 of members (18 of 31) agreeing to take it up, and the Republican majority writes the rules for 2027, including how much agenda power Goodwin keeps.

medicaid: Says she will push the Legislature to expand Medicaid, mostly federally funded, and strengthen rural hospitals (Jun and Nov 2026).
priorauth: Would ban insurers' bad-faith coverage denials, a related but narrower step than ending prior authorization; no insulin co-pay plan found (2026).
datactr: Would end over $1 billion in data center tax exemptions and impose a permit moratorium (2026).
ratefreeze: Would freeze residential electricity rates until large users pay for the infrastructure they need (2026).
gastax: $1,500 payment to every household and would suspend the gas tax until prices stabilize (2026).
renter: Platform would hold landlords accountable for AI-driven rent pricing and rent hikes without notice; she also backs cash back for renters (Jan 2026).
corphome: Would stop private equity and institutional investors buying up homes; her 2025 bill would cap investors at 10 single-family homes (2025-2026).
ptaxcorp: Would cut corporate subsidies to pay for property-tax cuts (2026).
ptax: Commits to cutting homeowner property taxes and ultimately eliminating residential property taxes, plus cash back for renters (2026).
mctax: Candidate questionnaire says she would cut taxes for families and small businesses, without a specific income-tax mechanism (2026).
vouchers: Pledges to end private-school vouchers and stop state takeovers of districts (2026).
ice: Opposed forcing local police to help enforce immigration law (2017) and criticizes federal ICE tactics; related, not sensitive-location rules (2026).
guard: Criticized Abbott for sending Texas Guard troops to Chicago and Portland as 'political theater' (Oct 2025).
fraud: Pledges to audit and cancel corrupt vendor contracts and end no-bid contracts, narrower than an inspector general overhaul (2026).
house: 'Expand the supply of homes Texans can afford' (2026).
roe: On the Roe anniversary she vowed to end Texas's abortion ban and guarantee women's right to privacy and care as governor (Jan 2026).

ss.name: Georgia
ss.rule: Georgia's constitution requires a majority of all 56 senators (29) for final passage, whoever is absent. The lieutenant governor presides but casts no tie-breaking vote on bills.

medicaid: Full Medicaid expansion is an immediate priority; would end Georgia Pathways (2026).
drugbd: Would create a Georgia Rx Savings Board to tackle prescription drug costs (2026 campaign issues page).
priorauth: Her CARE health plan would streamline prior authorization and cut paperwork burdens; no ban or insulin cap (Apr 2026).
aca: CARE plan pledges targeted state premium support and other backstops for ACA enrollees after federal subsidies lapsed; no dollar figure (Apr 2026).
datactr: Calls for a pause on new data centers until the state sets rules (2026); not a cost-recovery plan.
gastax: Backs suspending Georgia's gas tax to ease fuel costs (Apr 2026 debate); a specific 28-cent target was not verified.
trust: Proposes a statewide affordable housing trust fund (2026).
downpay: Would expand down payment and renter assistance (2026 campaign issues page).
corphome: Would crack down on corporate single-family landlords (2026).
ptax: Campaign lists a property tax and insurance relief plan; opposes abolishing property taxes; details not published (Sept 2026).
mctax: Would exempt teachers from state income tax and offer veteran/military retiree relief; narrower than a broad middle-class cut (Apr 2026).
childcare: Lists universal child care as a goal on her campaign issues page (2026).
teacher: Would raise average starting teacher pay from $48,000 to $60,000 and end state income tax for teachers (Aug-Sept 2026).
ice: Opposes Trump immigration tactics and as mayor ended the city jail's ICE detention contract (2018, noted Apr 2026); related, nothing on sensitive locations.
guard: Said nothing justifies sending the Guard into Atlanta, calling Trump's talk 'inflammatory' (Oct 2026); pledged to review Georgia's troops in D.C.
house: Proposes a 'Georgia Housing Fast Track' to streamline permitting; no zoning or preemption plan (2026 campaign).
roe: Vows to fight to restore abortion rights and repeal Georgia's six-week 'heartbeat' law (Apr 2026 debate; campaign site).

sch.full: Re-elect Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader

aca.full: Restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits

medicaid.full: Repeal the OBBBA Medicaid cuts and work requirements

drugneg.full: Expand Medicare drug price negotiation (SMART Prices Act)

priorauth.full: Curb prior authorization (Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act)

roe.full: Codify Roe: the Women's Health Protection Act

gouge.full: Ban grocery price-gouging and limit surveillance pricing

meat.full: Break up meatpackers (Family Grocery and Farmer Relief Act) and block grocery mergers

datactr.full: Make data centers pay their own power costs and cap utility hikes

childcare.full: Cap child care at 7% of income / universal child care

toptax.full: Repeal the OBBBA top-bracket cuts and close billionaire loopholes

pfl.full: National paid family and medical leave

downpay.full: Down payment assistance for first-time buyers

wage.full: Raise the minimum wage ($15–$25) and expand overtime

pro.full: PRO Act (Protecting the Right to Organize)

stock.full: Ban congressional stock trading: the Peters–Hawley–Merkley–Ossoff bill, covering the President and VP

pacs.full: Ban corporate PACs and super PACs

termlim.full: Constitutional amendment for congressional term or age limits

heg.full: Convict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if the House impeaches him

ice.full: Rein in ICE: no masks, body cameras, visible ID, judicial warrants, right to sue

tariff.full: End the tariff emergencies and pass the Trade Review Act

why.fil: Changing the rule by precedent (the 'nuclear option') needs a simple majority. At 50–50, VP Vance breaks the tie against it, so 51 is the real number.
why.sch: Decided by secret ballot inside the Democratic caucus in early December. Schumer needs a simple majority of caucus members; Republicans don't vote.
why.isr: Arms-sale disapproval resolutions are privileged under the Arms Export Control Act, so they can't be filibustered: 51 passes the Senate. Trump would veto, which takes 67 to override.
why.iran: War Powers Act joint resolutions get expedited, filibuster-proof votes, so 51 passes the Senate. Trump would veto, which takes 67 to override.
why.tariff: Resolutions ending a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act are privileged, so ending the tariff emergencies takes 51. The Trade Review Act itself is an ordinary bill (60 while the filibuster stands). Trump would veto either; 67 overrides.
why.heg: Removing an impeached official takes a two-thirds vote of senators present (67 if all 100 vote). The filibuster doesn't apply, and the president has no role.
why.termlim: A constitutional amendment needs two-thirds of the Senate (67) and the House, then ratification by 38 states. The president has no role.

A state board to negotiate prescription drug prices
A state public health insurance option
Cancel medical debt and keep it off credit reports
End prior authorization and insulin co-pays
Backfill lost ACA subsidies with state money
Make data centers pay their full costs
Utility accountability: caps on fees, limits on utility influence
Emergency rate freezes and bill credits
Push regulators and the grid operator to cap prices
Cut gas taxes or send direct payments
Ease zoning and building rules, including statewide preemption
Down payment help and a broker-fee ban
Pay for property-tax cuts by ending corporate giveaways
State child and working-family tax credits
End state tax on Social Security and seniors
Fund public schools fully instead of vouchers
Write abortion rights into state law
Keep a federalized National Guard out of the state without the governor's consent

sen.heg: If the House impeaches Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a Senate trial decides whether to remove him; a Republican-led impeachment resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie is pending.
sen.fil: Changes Senate rules so most bills can pass with a simple majority instead of 60 votes, which would let a Democratic majority move much of this agenda without Republican support.
sen.sch: Decides whether Chuck Schumer stays as leader of the Senate Democratic caucus, which shapes who sets the floor schedule and the party's strategy for the next two years.
sen.m4a: Replaces private insurance with a single public plan covering every American, ending premiums and deductibles but requiring large new federal taxes to pay for it.
sen.aca: Brings back the larger ACA marketplace subsidies that expired after 2025, lowering premiums for millions of people who buy their own coverage.
sen.medicaid: Reverses the Medicaid funding cuts and new work requirements in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, keeping coverage for people projected to lose it.
sen.drugneg: Lets Medicare negotiate prices on many more drugs each year, which would lower costs for seniors and federal spending on prescriptions.
sen.priorauth: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to approve routine care faster through electronic prior authorization, cutting delays for patients and paperwork for doctors.
sen.roe: Creates a federal right to provide and receive abortion care, overriding most state bans and restrictions passed since Roe v. Wade was overturned.
sen.gouge: Makes excessive grocery price hikes illegal and limits stores' use of personal data to charge different shoppers different prices.
sen.meat: Forces the biggest meatpackers to sell off lines of business and blocks new grocery mergers, aiming to restore competition and lower meat prices.
sen.gastax: Temporarily stops the 18.4-cent-per-gallon federal gas tax, giving drivers a modest break at the pump at the cost of highway funding.
sen.datactr: Requires data centers to cover the full cost of the power and grid upgrades they need and limits utility rate increases, so households aren't left paying for the AI boom.
sen.ctc: Makes the Child Tax Credit larger and available in full to low-income families, which cut child poverty sharply when it was temporarily expanded in 2021.
sen.childcare: Caps what families pay for child care at 7% of their income and funds more providers, moving toward child care that every family can afford.
sen.toptax: Undoes the 2025 tax cuts for the highest earners and closes loopholes used by billionaires, raising revenue for other priorities.
sen.pfl: Guarantees workers paid time off to care for a new child, a sick relative, or their own illness, funded through a national insurance program.
sen.downpay: Gives first-time and first-generation homebuyers federal help with a down payment, making it easier for renters to buy a home.
sen.wage: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to between $15 and $25 an hour and expands overtime pay, giving raises to millions of low-wage workers.
sen.pro: Makes it easier for workers to form unions and bargain, and adds penalties for employers who illegally fight organizing drives.
sen.repair: Requires equipment makers to give farmers and independent shops the tools, parts, and software needed to fix their own machines.
sen.stock: Bars members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President from trading individual stocks while in office, removing a major conflict of interest.
sen.gerry: Bans partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts nationwide, so maps can't be drawn to lock in one party's advantage.
sen.dcpr: Admits Washington, DC and Puerto Rico as states, giving their residents full voting representation in Congress and adding four senators.
sen.pacs: Bans corporate PAC contributions and super PACs, cutting off the main channels for unlimited corporate and outside money in federal elections.
sen.termlim: Amends the Constitution to cap how long members of Congress can serve, which needs two-thirds of both chambers and approval by 38 states.
sen.imm: Overhauls the immigration system by pairing border security with a path to legal status for long-time undocumented residents.
sen.ice: Sets new limits on immigration agents, including no masks, visible ID, body cameras, judicial warrants, and the right to sue over abuses.
sen.isr: Puts conditions on U.S. military aid to Israel, such as limits on offensive weapons, tied to how the weapons are used in Gaza.
sen.iran: Uses the War Powers Resolution to require congressional approval for continued U.S. military action against Iran.
sen.tariff: Ends the emergency declarations behind the current tariffs and requires Congress to approve new ones, which would lower import costs for businesses and shoppers.
sen.ai: Sets federal safety and accountability rules for AI and keeps states free to pass their own protections.

gov.medicaid: Extends Medicaid to low-income adults in states that haven't expanded and raises payments to providers, adding coverage and helping rural hospitals stay open.
gov.drugbd: Creates a state board that can set upper payment limits on high-cost prescription drugs, lowering what patients and health plans pay.
gov.pubopt: Offers a state-backed health plan anyone can buy, adding a lower-cost choice and competition in the individual insurance market.
gov.meddebt: Buys up and erases residents' medical debt and bars it from credit reports, so illness doesn't wreck people's ability to rent or borrow.
gov.priorauth: Ends insurer pre-approval rules for routine care and caps or eliminates insulin co-pays, speeding treatment and cutting out-of-pocket costs.
gov.aca: Uses state money to replace the federal ACA subsidies that expired after 2025, keeping marketplace premiums affordable.
gov.datactr: Makes data centers pay their full power, water, and grid costs and ends their tax breaks, so households don't subsidize them through higher bills.
gov.utility: Caps utility fees and limits utilities' political spending and lobbying costs on customers' bills, giving regulators more power to hold down rates.
gov.ratefreeze: Freezes utility rates or orders bill credits during an affordability emergency, giving households immediate relief on energy costs.
gov.pricecap: Pushes state regulators and the regional grid operator to cap wholesale electricity prices, limiting how much power-market spikes reach customers' bills.
gov.gastax: Cuts or suspends the state gas tax, or sends households direct payments, to offset high fuel prices.
gov.house: Loosens zoning and building rules, sometimes overriding local limits, so more homes can be built and rents and prices can come down.
gov.eohousing: Uses executive orders and emergency powers to speed up permits and financing for housing already in the pipeline.
gov.trust: Creates dedicated funds or bonds that finance the construction of affordable homes and apartments.
gov.downpay: Gives first-time buyers help with down payments and bans renters from paying brokers' fees, lowering the upfront cost of a home or apartment.
gov.renter: Adds renter protections such as caps on security deposits and junk fees and bans on algorithmic rent-fixing.
gov.corphome: Limits how many single-family homes large investors can buy, leaving more starter homes for families.
gov.ptaxcorp: Pays for homeowner property-tax cuts by ending tax breaks and subsidies for corporations.
gov.ptax: Targets property-tax relief at homeowners and seniors through larger exemptions, credits, or rebates.
gov.mctax: Cuts state income taxes for middle-class families, for example through a bigger standard deduction or no tax on tips and overtime.
gov.ctc: Creates or expands a state child tax credit or earned income credit, putting cash directly into working families' pockets.
gov.sstax: Stops taxing Social Security and other retirement income, lowering taxes for seniors.
gov.millionaire: Adds a higher income tax rate on earnings above $1 million, raising revenue for housing, schools, or other priorities.
gov.prek: Offers free pre-K to every four-year-old (and sometimes three-year-olds), helping kids start school ready and saving parents child care costs.
gov.childcare: Builds a child care system every family can afford, often by capping costs as a share of income and funding providers directly.
gov.teacher: Raises teacher pay, such as a higher minimum starting salary, to recruit and keep teachers.
gov.vouchers: Opposes or repeals private-school voucher programs and puts that money into fully funding public schools.
gov.pfml: Creates a state insurance program that gives workers paid time off for a new child, a sick relative, or their own illness.
gov.wage: Raises the state minimum wage to $15 an hour, giving raises to the lowest-paid workers.
gov.roe: Writes the right to abortion into state law or the state constitution, protecting access regardless of federal action.
gov.ice: Bars immigration agents from schools, hospitals, courthouses, and places of worship without a judicial warrant.
gov.guard: Opposes a president federalizing the National Guard, or sending in another state's troops, over the governor's objection, through lawsuits, refusals, and state laws. State laws can bar other states' troops sent under Title 32, but not a president's Title 10 federalization, which only courts have checked.
gov.npv: Joins the interstate compact to award the state's electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner, which takes effect once states with 270 votes sign on.
gov.avr: Registers eligible citizens to vote automatically when they deal with state agencies like the DMV, unless they opt out.
gov.fraud: Overhauls oversight of state programs with surprise audits and an independent inspector general to catch fraud and waste.

factions.Presidential Hopefuls: The 2028 draft class, and they're already running their own sets. Three of the four put distance between themselves and Trump within days of the loss (Vance flatly blamed the war; Hawley and DeSantis went after Senate leadership), while Rubio is the lone guy still setting screens for the boss.
factions.Media voices: The podcast-and-cable ecosystem that actually sets the movement's agenda, and it's splitting the fastest. Carlson declared the Trump era over and Shapiro called it a repudiation, Turning Point's Erika Kirk pointed to prices and the war but warned against infighting, and Hannity and Loomer stayed firmly in Trump's corner.
factions.Hawks: Peace-through-strength traditionalists, the wing most tied to the Iran war. Cruz called the night a Watergate-level repudiation and says the war has dragged on too long, Haley went full critic, and on Israel nobody here is giving an inch.
factions.Pragmatists and Dissenters: The told-you-so caucus of Republicans who kept Trump at arm's length all along. Christie declared "the Trump era is over," Murkowski wants Congress's war powers back, and Ayotte just showed you can survive a blue wave by running as yourself.
factions.Trump Loyalists: The franchise and its lifers. Their answer to a wipeout was promoting Stephen Miller and keeping Hegseth; even Trump's admission that the war and gas prices hurt came with an "emphatic yes" that he'd do it again. Budd, Landry, and Reeves conceded the damage without blaming him.
factions.Tea Party/Freedom Caucus: The deficit hawks and libertarian gadflies, now leading the revolt against a quick leadership vote: Ron Johnson forced a debrief meeting with Lee and Rick Scott, and Chip Roy says Republicans "dropped the ball." Rand Paul blames deficits, tariffs and the war, and Massie is pushing Hegseth impeachment articles.
factions.New Right: The post-liberal, pro-worker, anti-H-1B wing that was supposed to inherit MAGA. Banks says there's "no way to spin" the loss and wants a frank reckoning before leaders are chosen, Moreno wants a "Last Supper" lame-duck sprint, and Schmitt has stayed on offense against Democrats instead of talking about the loss.
factions.Institutionalists: The leadership class and the governors who keep the lights on. Mostly they're hedging and lining up for minority-leadership jobs (Barrasso sees "clear lessons" but names no culprit); Lankford is the outlier, calling it a referendum on Trump and ICE, while Thune and Kemp actually moved closer to the party line.

boast.John Thune: Defended the record: taxes, border, Cabinet, judges.

field.h: The 2028 field is breaking. The Cabinet isn't.
field.b: Vance (−6.3), Cruz (−4.2), Hawley (−3.9), and DeSantis (−3.3) all moved away from Trump within days. Rubio, still in the Cabinet, is the only hopeful holding with him.

iran.h: The Iran war is the position they're abandoning.
iran.b: Nine Republicans from six factions broke with the war. The only four still defending it are Trump and his inner circle: Rubio, Hegseth, and Sanders.

romney.b: Three are going harder, mostly on H-1B visas, and Chip Roy is doubling down on enforcement; only Lankford is pushing back, and only on ICE tactics. Like 2012's promised pivot, the leftward move isn't coming.

middle.b: Republicans scoring 8 or above on the Trump scale fell from 19 to 12, while those at 3 or below jumped from 5 to 13. The party is sorting away from Trump, not abandoning him.

prices.b: 17 of the 33 who gave a reason pointed to prices and cost of living; only 7 blamed Trump himself. Expect an affordability pivot, not a break with him.

tariffs.b: Three free-marketers from three factions (Cruz, Paul, Lankford) broke on tariffs, and not one Republican doubled down on them.

voices.h: The voices are outrunning the officials.
voices.b: Hosts and outside voices moved about twice as far from Trump as elected and appointed officials did, on average. The ideas tend to lead the votes.

senate.h: The Senate GOP is turning on its own leadership.
senate.b: Only 4 of the 18 Republican senators on the list have said nothing. Five pushed to delay the leadership vote, and 7 moved at least a point away from Trump; leader Thune moved toward him.

israel.b: Only Trump and Vance have shifted on Israel. The Hawks and Loyalists haven't budged from strongly pro-Israel, so the fight is at the top, not the base.

partners.h: Iran war powers is the biggest bipartisan opening.
partners.b: Nine Republicans who broke on the war map onto the Iran war powers measure, the most for any Agenda item. Tariff emergencies is next, with three.

field2.h: The 2028 field is breaking with Trump, except Rubio.
field2.b: Vance (−6.3), Cruz (−4.2), Hawley (−3.9), and DeSantis (−3.3) moved away, mostly by blaming his policies rather than him: Vance the Iran war, Cruz tariffs and the war, Hawley costs, DeSantis a do-nothing Senate. Rubio, still in the Cabinet, defended the war and holds at 10.

senate2.h: Senate Republicans want a reckoning first.
senate2.b: 14 of the 18 GOP senators on the list have now spoken, and 7 moved at least a point away from Trump, led by Lankford, Cruz, and Hawley. Johnson, Lee, Rick Scott, Budd, and Banks want a debrief before leaders are chosen. Only Thune moved toward Trump; Cotton, Schmitt, Wicker, and Tim Scott are still silent.

bipart.h: Iran, corruption, and tariffs are bipartisan openings.
bipart.b: The widest GOP breaks: the Iran war (9 Republicans across 6 factions), corruption and the Epstein files (6 across 5), and tariffs (3, with no defenders). The likeliest places for early deals.
